title: The Charts and the Temple: Hilma af Klint, the Five, and the Twenty-Year Embargo
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Karlberg Palace, Solna: the birth at the war academy
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of October a fourth child is born to Victor af Klint, naval officer, and Mathilda Sonntag, in the halls of Karlberg Palace outside Stockholm, where the Royal War Academy trains army and naval cadets together under one roof. They name her Hilma. The house is full of charts and dividers. Her father teaches men to fix a point on open water. The daughter will spend her working life fixing points on surfaces nobody has charted, and she keeps the draughtsman's habit of labelling every one.
suggested_refs: Karlberg Palace, Solna, seat of the Royal War Academy (Krigsakademien) from 1792

stops.name: Hanmora, Adelso: the summers on Lake Malaren
stops.date_confidence: decade only (1860s-1870s); month and day defaulted; farm building not geolocated in any source reached, pin at island centroid
stops.campa: Summers take the af Klint children west to Hanmora, a farm on Adelso in Lake Malaren, an island that holds Viking royal ground at Hovgarden within sight of the water. Hilma spends the seasons close to the shore with a pencil, drawing plants and animals as they are, leaf by leaf. She is drawing specimens before she is drawing anything else. Forty years on, the spirals and biomorphic forms she paints under dictation will still be built the way a specimen sheet is built, one observed structure set beside another.
suggested_refs: Hanmora farm and the Viking-age royal ground at Hovgarden, Adelso

stops.name: Stockholm, the seances of Bertha Valerius
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown; ordering against her sister's death in 1880 disputed between sources; meeting address unlocated, pin at central Stockholm
stops.campa: At seventeen she begins attending seances led by Bertha Valerius, court photographer and medium, one of the women who carried spiritualism into respectable Stockholm drawing rooms. Within a year her younger sister Hermina is dead. The sources place the two events side by side and disagree about which came first, so whether the grief opened the door or found it already open is not settled. From this year the seance is a fixed part of her week, and it stays one for the rest of her life.
suggested_refs: Bertha Valerius, court photographer and medium, and the spiritualist drawing rooms of 1870s Stockholm
sources: TheArtStory, 'Hilma af Klint: Life and Legacy'

stops.name: Tekniska skolan, Stockholm: the enrolment under Kerstin Cardon
stops.date_confidence: year attested by sv.wikipedia; an earlier pass gave 1879, which is the seance year duplicated onto the wrong event; historic building coordinates approximate
stops.campa: She enrols at Tekniska skolan in central Stockholm, the technical school that will become Konstfack, and studies portrait painting under Kerstin Cardon. Two educations now run in parallel and neither interrupts the other: the drawing board by day, the darkened room by evening. Nothing in her coursework marks her out from any competent portraitist of her generation, and nothing is meant to. The public identity she builds here, landscape and portrait painter, is the one she will present to Sweden for the next sixty years.
suggested_refs: Tekniska skolan, Stockholm, later Konstfack; the teaching of Kerstin Cardon

stops.name: Konstakademien, Stockholm: admitted at twenty
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown; coordinate from en.wikipedia's Fredsgatan reading, correcting an earlier plot 250 m east
stops.campa: At twenty she is admitted to the Royal Academy of Fine Arts on Fredsgatan, in the building the Academy has occupied since 1780. Women have been accepted since 1864, so she is not the first, but she belongs to the first generations allowed the full academic course rather than a shortened ladies' version. Among the students she meets Anna Cassel, who will be her closest collaborator for forty years, at the easel and later in the seance room. The certificate she will leave with licenses portrait and landscape work, and that is the only work Sweden ever sees from her.
suggested_refs: The Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts on Fredsgatan, occupied since 1780; the admission of women students from 1864
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts'

stops.name: Konstakademien, Stockholm: the honours and the stipend
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown
stops.campa: Five years of portraiture, botanical drawing, and landscape end in graduation with honours and a state stipend. She can render a face and a plant stem to exhibition standard, and she has learned to finish what she starts. Swedish painting of the 1880s is turning toward plein-air naturalism and the national landscape, and she can do all of it. Her exhibited work over the coming decades will be exactly this and nothing else. What she is about to begin, she will show to almost no one who was in this room.
suggested_refs: The Konstakademien graduation records of 1887 and the state stipend attached to them
sources: TheArtStory, 'Hilma af Klint: Life and Legacy'

stops.name: Ateljebyggnaden, Hamngatan 5: the studio granted
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month inferred from the graduation, day defaulted
stops.campa: The stipend brings a room: a studio in the Ateljebyggnaden, the artists' building at Hamngatan 5 between the street and Kungstradgarden, in the middle of Stockholm. She keeps it for decades. Every canvas of the Temple cycle will be painted here, and the largest of them will be rolled through this door on its way out. Rudolf Steiner will stand in this room in 1908 and tell her what he thinks of the work. The money is awarded for conventional painting. What it buys is the room where she stops painting conventionally.
suggested_refs: The Ateljebyggnaden at Hamngatan 5, Stockholm, studio of the entire Temple cycle

segments.name: De Fem and the High Masters

stops.name: Stockholm, the Edelweiss Society
stops.date_confidence: membership dated 1896-1897 by sv.wikipedia, overlapping the founding of De Fem; an earlier pass gave c.1889-1896, unsourced; meeting address unlocated, pin at central Stockholm
stops.campa: She takes part in Edelweissforbundet, a Stockholm spiritualist circle where table-tipping and mediumship are practised among a wider set of women than the group she is about to form. The society supplies the method: contact with a guide, and a transcript taken down as the guide speaks. The sources reached give her membership as 1896 to 1897, which puts it alongside the founding of De Fem rather than before it. Which came first inside that year is not established, and the order between them is left open.
suggested_refs: Edelweissforbundet, the Stockholm spiritualist society from which De Fem emerged

stops.name: Stockholm, the founding of De Fem
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown; an earlier pass placed the meetings at Engelbrektsgatan 31, which no source reached supports, so the pin is an unlocated central-Stockholm plot
stops.campa: Five women constitute themselves a working group: af Klint, Anna Cassel, Cornelia Cederberg, Sigrid Hedman, Mathilda Nilsson. They call themselves De Fem, the Five. Each session opens with prayer, meditation, a Christian sermon, and exegesis of a New Testament passage, and only then is contact sought. Automatic writing follows, then automatic drawing. The first non-figurative marks in af Klint's hand appear in these notebooks, some fourteen years before Kandinsky's canvases carry the claim of being first. Where in Stockholm they met is not documented in any source reached.
suggested_refs: The surviving notebooks of De Fem, 1896-1908, Hilma af Klint Foundation

stops.name: Stockholm, the message of Gregor
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day defaulted, the message not individually dated in any source reached
stops.campa: Among the entities the group records are the ones they call the High Masters, Hoga Mastare: Amaliel, Gregor, Ananda, Clemens, Esther. Gregor speaks about a kind of knowing that is not sensory, not intellectual, not emotional, and the women write it down verbatim, the way stenographers write, without interpretation. Ten years before the first Temple canvas the programme is already stated: the pictures to come will be about a knowledge that has no organ. The primary notebook behind this message was not located, and the wording here is as it is quoted at second hand.
stops.quote: All the knowledge that is not of the senses, not of the intellect, not of the heart but is the property that exclusively belongs to the deepest aspect of your being ... the knowledge of your spirit
stops.quote_source: Message attributed to the spirit guide Gregor, recorded by De Fem, quoted in en.wikipedia, 'Hilma af Klint', footnote 16 (ellipsis in the source as quoted)
suggested_refs: The De Fem seance transcripts naming the Hoga Mastare: Amaliel, Gregor, Ananda, Clemens, Esther

stops.name: Stockholm, the Theosophical Society
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Hilma af Klint Foundation gives May 1904, sv.wikipedia gives 1905; the Foundation adopted, the variant kept on record; lodge address unconfirmed, pin at central Stockholm
stops.campa: In May she joins the Stockholm lodge of the Theosophical Society, the body Helena Blavatsky founded and Annie Besant now leads from Adyar. The private seance practice acquires a public doctrine: planes of consciousness, root races, an evolution of spirit whose stages are numbered and can therefore be drawn. Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine gives her a cosmology large enough to need diagrams. The Foundation dates the joining to 1904 and Swedish Wikipedia to 1905; the earlier date is used here, with the later one kept on record.
suggested_refs: The Stockholm lodge of the Theosophical Society and the Swedish reception of Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine
sources: TheArtStory, 'Hilma af Klint: Life and Legacy'

stops.name: Ateljebyggnaden, Hamngatan 5: the commission from Amaliel
stops.date_confidence: month attested by the Hilma af Klint Foundation (January 1906), day defaulted; an earlier pass carried an unsourced 1904 directive to paint on the astral plane, dropped
stops.campa: In January, at forty-four, af Klint records receiving a commission from a being who names itself Amaliel: to make paintings for a temple. She accepts. Nothing in her training prepares her for the scale or for the abandonment of the figure, and she does not appear to hesitate. The work begins in November. Over nine years it will run to 193 pictures, made in a rented studio in the centre of a capital city, by a woman who continues meanwhile to exhibit landscapes and to be known in Stockholm as a landscape painter.
suggested_refs: The Hilma af Klint Foundation chronology of the Amaliel commission, January 1906
sources: TheArtStory, 'Hilma af Klint: Life and Legacy'

stops.name: Ateljebyggnaden, Hamngatan 5: Primordial Chaos
stops.date_confidence: month attested by the Foundation as the start of painting, day defaulted; the group of twenty-six spans 1906-1907
stops.campa: The first group is twenty-six small panels she calls Primordial Chaos, worked in blue, yellow, and green, spirals and shell forms and the split ovum. She paints, by her own account, fast and without correction. Whatever else is happening in that room, it is not the academic procedure she was trained in for five years: no preliminary drawing and nothing painted twice. Two years from now Rudolf Steiner will look at everything she has made and approve of this group alone, calling it the best of it, symbolically.
suggested_refs: The Primordial Chaos group, twenty-six works, Hilma af Klint Foundation
sources: TheArtStory, 'Hilma af Klint: Life and Legacy'

stops.name: Ateljebyggnaden, Hamngatan 5: The Ten Largest
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown
stops.campa: In a single year she paints ten pictures on the four stages of human life, childhood, youth, adulthood, old age, each about two and a half metres by three and a quarter, on paper laid out on the studio floor. They are the largest abstract paintings anyone has made. The colour is soft, almost nursery-bright; the forms are seed cases, blossoms, script that is not a language. She works on the floor because no easel will take them, and by her own written account she does not change a stroke.
stops.quote: The pictures were painted directly through me, without any preliminary drawings, and with great force. I had no idea what the paintings were supposed to depict; nevertheless I worked swiftly and surely, without changing a single brush stroke.
stops.quote_source: Hilma af Klint, notebook entry, English translation quoted in en.wikipedia, 'Hilma af Klint', footnote 18; Swedish original verified against sv.wikipedia, footnote 24
suggested_refs: The Ten Largest, 1907, ten works of roughly 240 by 320 cm, tempera on paper mounted on canvas

stops.name: Stockholm, De Fem dissolve
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Foundation gives dissolution in early 1908, sv.wikipedia ends the membership span in 1907; an earlier pass gave 1906, unsupported
stops.campa: After twelve years of weekly sessions the group breaks up in the early months of the year. The Foundation gives the dissolution as early 1908; Swedish Wikipedia ends the membership in 1907. Whatever the month, the collective phase is over and the commission has already passed to one pair of hands. Cassel stays close to af Klint for the rest of both their lives, as friend, as lender, and eventually as the owner of the house and the studio on Munso where the work ends up stored.
suggested_refs: The closing records of De Fem, 1907-1908

stops.name: Ateljebyggnaden, Hamngatan 5: Rudolf Steiner in the studio
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established in any source reached; the exact wording of Steiner's remarks varies between secondary accounts
stops.campa: Rudolf Steiner comes to Stockholm and is brought to Hamngatan to see the Temple paintings. He looks. He approves of Primordial Chaos and of little else, tells her that painting as a passive medium is the wrong road, and warns that nobody will understand this work for fifty years. The accounts differ on how long a silence he advised. She stops. Four years pass before she paints another picture in the cycle, and what he meant by the visit is never settled.
suggested_refs: Julia Voss, Hilma af Klint: A Biography (2020), on the 1908 studio visit; Ake Fant's earlier accounts of the same
sources: TheArtStory, 'Hilma af Klint: Life and Legacy'
Julia Voss, Hilma af Klint: A Biography (2020), cited at second hand, text not reached

stops.name: Ateljebyggnaden, Hamngatan 5: the second phase resumed
stops.date_confidence: year attested as the resumption, not the completion; the hiatus runs 1908-1912 and the second phase 1912-1915
stops.campa: After four years of silence she takes up the commission again, now working with preliminary studies and a more deliberate hand than the trance method of the first phase. The Swan, the Dove, and the Altarpieces are all ahead of her. She is fifty. In the intervening years she has kept the studio, and no source reached says she showed anyone what was inside it. The second phase runs to 1915 and produces the work that will hang, a century later, in the rotunda of a museum on Fifth Avenue.
suggested_refs: The 1908-1912 production hiatus and the second-phase working method with preliminary studies

stops.name: Malmo, the Baltic Exhibition
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the showing rests on a single secondary account; month and day taken from the exhibition's opening, hall not identified, pin at the Baltic Exhibition grounds now under Pildammsparken
stops.campa: She sends a landscape to the Baltic Exhibition at Malmo, a regional survey of Nordic and Baltic art, and it hangs in the same exhibition as early abstract work by Wassily Kandinsky. Nothing in her submission would tell a visitor that the largest abstract paintings in Europe are rolled up in a Stockholm studio belonging to the woman who painted this competent Swedish landscape. She maintains the double life exactly, and the record of this showing rests on one secondary account and no catalogue reached.
suggested_refs: The Baltic Exhibition, Malmo, 1914, and its catalogue of Nordic and Baltic art
sources: TheArtStory, 'Hilma af Klint: Life and Legacy'

stops.name: Ateljebyggnaden, Hamngatan 5: the Swan
stops.date_confidence: attested as October 1914 to March 1915; an earlier pass gave 1914 alone
stops.campa: From October to March she paints the Swan: twenty-four pictures in which two birds, one white and one black, meet, overlap, interpenetrate, and finally disappear into pure geometry. The series is the clearest demonstration in the whole cycle of what she means by evolution, a figurative pair driven stage by stage into abstraction until the subject is gone and only the operation remains. Europe has been at war for two months. The studio does not register it.
suggested_refs: The Swan series, twenty-four paintings, October 1914 to March 1915
sources: TheArtStory, 'Hilma af Klint: Life and Legacy'

stops.name: Ateljebyggnaden, Hamngatan 5: the Dove, the Altarpieces, and the end of the guidance
stops.date_confidence: year attested as the completion of the cycle; month inferred from the close of the Swan series, day defaulted
stops.campa: The Dove group and the three Altarpieces close the commission. The last of them is a golden pyramid pointed at a black disc, the only picture in the cycle that looks like an ending. Af Klint records that the guidance which directed the work now ceases. Nine years, 193 paintings, no exhibition, no buyer, no critic. In 1916 she paints the Parsifal series on her own initiative, and the difference between commissioned and uncommissioned work becomes, for the first time in a decade, a question she has to answer herself.
suggested_refs: The three Altarpieces of 1915, closing works of the Paintings for the Temple; the Parsifal series of 1916
sources: TheArtStory, 'Hilma af Klint: Life and Legacy'

stops.name: Munso, the studio at Bona
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown; coordinate corrected from an earlier plot 6 km north of the island, in open water; exact studio site not pinpointed
stops.campa: Anna Cassel lends her three thousand kronor, later settled between them, to raise a studio on Munso at Bona, the island beside the Adelso of her childhood across the same water. She had bought the summer house at Furuheim four years earlier. The new building is inaugurated this year and it will outlast her: after 1944 it is not a workroom but a store. In the same period she begins Studier over Sjalslivet, Studies of the Life of the Soul, a manuscript that runs past twelve hundred pages and is never published.
suggested_refs: The studio building at Bona fideikommiss, Munso, inaugurated 1917; the unpublished manuscript Studier over Sjalslivet
sources: TheArtStory, 'Hilma af Klint: Life and Legacy'

stops.name: Furuheim, Munso: the mother brought to the island
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown; an earlier pass misplaced this caregiving into the 1908-1912 hiatus
stops.campa: She moves to Furuheim with her mother Mathilda, who is going blind. The war ends that autumn. The household on the island is quiet, and the work she makes here is small, botanical, kept in notebooks rather than stretched on frames. The monumental decade is over. She is fifty-six, unmarried, unexhibited in the only work she considers her real work, and living on an island in Lake Malaren caring for a woman who cannot see the pictures. The studio at Bona stands a short walk off across the fields, and the rolled canvases of nine years are already accumulating inside it.
suggested_refs: Furuheim, the af Klint summer house on Munso, bought 1913 and occupied year-round from 1918

stops.name: Munso, the mother's death and the change of societies
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown
stops.campa: Mathilda af Klint dies. In the same year her daughter leaves the Theosophical Society and joins the Anthroposophical Society, following Rudolf Steiner out of Annie Besant's Adyar and into a Christ-centred esotericism with a building of its own in Switzerland. She is fifty-eight and free of the household for the first time in her adult life. What she does with the freedom is travel. Within months she is at Dornach, and for the next ten years she goes back every year.
suggested_refs: The 1912-1913 rupture between Steiner's German section and Besant's Adyar, and its Swedish membership consequences
sources: TheArtStory, 'Hilma af Klint: Life and Legacy'

stops.name: Helsingborg, the winters on the Oresund
stops.date_confidence: start year attested as 1920 onward; no month is given in any source reached, and the day is set inside 1920 to hold the stops in travel order against the June visit to Dornach; address not given, pin at the city centre
stops.campa: From this year she keeps a seasonal rhythm: the island and Stockholm in the warm months, Helsingborg on the Oresund in the cold ones, at the opposite end of the country from everything else in her life. No source reached gives an address, and none states a reason for the choice. It is the pattern of a woman with a small income, no dependants, and no institution expecting her anywhere on any particular day. She keeps it for the last twenty-four years of her life.
suggested_refs: Helsingborg on the Oresund, af Klint's winter residence from 1920

stops.name: Goetheanum, Dornach: the hill above the Birs
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown; coordinate inherited unchanged from steiner.journey.json
stops.campa: She comes to the Jura hill above Dornach to see the first Goetheanum, Rudolf Steiner's double-domed house of carved wood on a concrete base, named for Goethe and raised through the war by volunteers from seventeen nations. Nothing in Swedish architecture is shaped like it: curved, non-rectilinear, every column a different plant-form of the same growth. She has been drawing forms of this kind alone in a Stockholm room for fourteen years. Here is a building that agrees with her, put up by people who will not look at what she painted.
suggested_refs: The first Goetheanum at Dornach, 1913-1922, and its carved planetary columns

stops.name: Dornach, Peggy Kloppers-Moltzer and the letter to Wendingen
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia gives 'around 1920'; month and day defaulted; an earlier pass named a companion, Elsa Cochius, who appears in no source reached and has been removed
stops.campa: At Dornach she meets Peggy Kloppers-Moltzer, a Dutch eurythmist, and through her writes to the editors of Wendingen in Amsterdam, the architecture and arts magazine, proposing an exhibition. Nothing comes of it. It is one of the very few times in her life she asks anyone for a wall, and the request goes to a Dutch avant-garde periodical rather than to a Swedish museum. She is fifty-eight and has been painting abstractly for fourteen years without a single wall.
suggested_refs: Wendingen, Amsterdam, and the unrealised af Klint exhibition proposal of the early 1920s

stops.name: Dornach, the Goetheanum burns
stops.date_confidence: fire attested to the night of 31 December 1922 to 1 January 1923; af Klint's presence not documented in any source reached; arson claimed but, per en.wikipedia, not proven
stops.campa: On New Year's Eve the first Goetheanum catches fire and burns through the night. By morning only the concrete base is standing. Arson is widely suspected and never proven. Whether af Klint is on the hill that night is not documented in any source reached, and no claim is made that she was. The building she recognised two years earlier is gone in a single night, and Steiner begins the model of its concrete successor within the year, a form even less like anything else in Europe than the first.
suggested_refs: The burning of the first Goetheanum, 31 December 1922 to 1 January 1923

stops.name: Dornach, whether the work should be destroyed
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the text's own '14 or 15 years ago' after the 1908 visit, giving 1922-1923; month and day defaulted; coordinate inherited from the Schreinerei pin in steiner.journey.json
stops.campa: She writes an account of the whole commission and puts a question to the Anthroposophical Society and to Steiner himself: whether the 193 paintings should be preserved or destroyed. The answer, as she records it, is that letting them disappear would be harmful and that they could be used. It is the only recorded moment at which the cycle nearly ended in a fire of its own. The text survives in a personal notebook quoted at second hand, and the archival original was never traced.
stops.quote: The execution of the work began a few years before Dr. Steiner first came to Sweden, and when I heard about him, it was immediately clear to me that he was the one who would confirm what I had perceived. Under the guidance of one, or perhaps several intelligences, the work is executed in a number of painted pictures, some very small, some very large. This logically constructed work contains an explanation of the evolution of mankind over vast periods of time. There are two reasons why I wish to interest the Anthroposophical Society in this work, namely, my absolute belief in the authenticity of the inspiration, and Dr. Steiner's confirmation of it when, 14 or 15 years ago, he looked at the first two series then completed, on which he made a detailed explanation. Since then the work has continued, and this year I have once again personally appealed to Dr. Steiner to find out about the work. Whether it should be preserved, or whether it should be destroyed. The answer was, that it would be detrimental to let it disappear and that it could be used and useful.
stops.quote_source: Hilma af Klint, personal notebook, quoted in en.wikipedia, 'Hilma af Klint', footnote 23; underlying archival document not independently traced
suggested_refs: The af Klint notebook appeal to the Anthroposophical Society, c. 1922-1923

stops.name: London, the World Conference on Spiritual Science
stops.date_confidence: year and conference attested; month from the pooled record, day defaulted; venue unconfirmed, pin at Rudolf Steiner House as the best candidate and flagged uncertain; the sea voyage and the exclusion story are unsupported and are not narrated
stops.campa: Her abstract paintings hang in public, in London, at the World Conference on Spiritual Science, an anthroposophical gathering on whose organising committee Peggy Kloppers-Moltzer sits. It is the only confirmed public showing of her non-figurative work in her lifetime. The hall is not identified in any source reached, and Rudolf Steiner House near Regent's Park was then still being built in stages, so the pin marks the best candidate rather than a fact. A story that she was excluded and then reinstated has no source and is not repeated.
suggested_refs: The 1928 World Conference on Spiritual Science, London, and its organising committee

stops.name: Dornach, the second Goetheanum standing
stops.date_confidence: completion year attested; month and day unknown; her annual visits run 1920-1930
stops.campa: The concrete Goetheanum is finished, three years after Steiner's death, a mass of angled planes on the same foundation as the burned original. Af Klint has been coming to this hill nearly every year since 1920, sometimes for months, studying anthroposophy, world religions, and botany, and cataloguing and photographing her own work as she goes. She is sixty-six. A claim that she gave paintings to the Goetheanum archive could not be corroborated anywhere and is left out. The visits end around 1930.
suggested_refs: The second Goetheanum, completed 1928, and the af Klint cataloguing and photography of her own corpus in these years

segments.name: Lund, Djursholm, and the Sealed Will

stops.name: Lund, the move with Thomasine Andersson
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown; address not given in any source reached, pin at the city centre
stops.campa: She moves to Lund with Thomasine Andersson, a nurse who has been with her since her mother's death and who stays to the end. It is the first time she lives in a university town rather than a capital or on an island. No source reached gives an address, or a reason beyond Andersson's own ties to the place. She is seventy-three and still working, in watercolour now, at a scale that fits on a table rather than on a floor. The Temple cycle has been rolled and crated for twenty years and she has stopped trying to find it a room.
suggested_refs: Thomasine Andersson, nurse and companion from 1920 to 1944

stops.name: Lund, the watercolours of the war
stops.date_confidence: contested and unresolved: sv.wikipedia dates the late watercolour activity to the 1930s and gives the whole period as 1920-1941, while the titles refer to events of 1940-1941; an earlier pass invented a precise 1935 that no source carries
stops.campa: Among the late watercolours are two that later commentators read as war pictures, one titled for the Blitz and one for fighting in the Mediterranean. The sources reached date her activity of these years to the 1930s, and the London Blitz begins in September 1940. The contradiction is printed rather than repaired: either the dating is loose or the titles are later attachments, and no reachable source settles it. Her late watercolour period is given as running from 1920 to 1941.
suggested_refs: The late af Klint watercolours, 1920-1941, including the two titled for the Blitz and the Mediterranean

stops.name: Djursholm, the cousin's villa
stops.date_confidence: year attested by sv.wikipedia; month and day unknown; an earlier pass had her living out her final years here rather than months
stops.campa: In her last year she leaves Lund for the villa of her cousin Hedvig af Klint in Djursholm, the planned garden suburb north of Stockholm. She is eighty-one. The paintings are elsewhere, crated. She has been taking instruction, by her own account, since a Stockholm room in the 1890s, and she has shown the results in public exactly once, in London, sixteen years ago. Djursholm's quiet planned streets are twelve kilometres and half a century from Hamngatan, where the first of the pictures was painted, and she will be here for months rather than years.
suggested_refs: The villa of Hedvig af Klint at Djursholm, the painter's last address

stops.name: Djursholm, the streetcar
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the vehicle is a streetcar per the Hilma af Klint Foundation, closing an earlier bus-versus-tram question and deleting an unsupported bicycle; sv.wikipedia registers the death administratively in Danderyd
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of October she is struck by a streetcar and dies of it, at eighty-one. Earlier accounts gave a bus and a bicycle; the Foundation specifies a tram, and a tram is what is recorded here. Swedish civil registration puts the death in Danderyd, the municipality of which Djursholm is a district. She dies as an obscure Swedish landscape painter of good family, which is what every obituary and every institution in the country believes her to be.
suggested_refs: The Hilma af Klint Foundation death record, 21 October 1944, Djursholm

stops.name: Galarvarvskyrkogarden, Djurgarden: the burial
stops.date_confidence: burial place attested, exact date not given in any source reached and set within the week after the death; coordinate corrected 700 m west from an earlier plot that fell in Djurgardsbrunnsviken
stops.campa: She is buried at Galarvarvskyrkogarden, the Galley Wharf cemetery on Djurgarden, in the family ground beside the naval father whose charts and dividers were the first drawn lines she ever saw. Her name goes on the stone with nothing added. The will read that autumn puts a twenty-year embargo on the abstract work. Nobody at the graveside knows that the largest body of abstract painting made before the First World War is in crates a few hours west, and nobody will know for a quarter of a century.
suggested_refs: The af Klint family plot at Galarvarvskyrkogarden, Djurgarden, Stockholm

stops.name: Stockholm, the will and the twenty years
stops.date_confidence: the terms are attested; the date of probate is not given in any source reached and is set to the month after the death
stops.campa: The will is read. More than 1,200 paintings and about 125 notebooks and diaries pass to her nephew, Vice Admiral Erik af Klint of the Royal Swedish Navy, with the condition that the abstract work not be shown for at least twenty years after her death. She gives no reason in the document. Steiner had told her in 1908 that fifty years would pass before anyone understood the work; she halves the sentence and imposes it herself, on her own estate, in her own hand.
suggested_refs: The 1944 testament of Hilma af Klint and its twenty-year exhibition embargo

stops.name: Moderna Museet, Stockholm: the boxes opened and the gift declined
stops.date_confidence: refusal attested to 1970, month and day unknown; the boxes are opened 'at the end of the 1960s' with no month given; coordinate corrected 350 m northwest from an earlier plot that fell in the water
stops.campa: The family opens the crates at the end of the 1960s: over 1,200 paintings, unseen, uncatalogued, absent from every history of abstraction written since. In 1970 they are offered as a gift to Moderna Museet on Skeppsholmen and the museum declines them. Where the boxes had stood for twenty-five years is not documented. The Munso studio is the usual answer, but Anna Cassel owned that building from 1932 and no reachable source follows the crates. Forty-three years later this same museum will launch the retrospective.
suggested_refs: The 1970 refusal of the af Klint donation by Moderna Museet, Skeppsholmen

stops.name: Stockholm, the Foundation established
stops.date_confidence: sv.wikipedia dates Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk to 1972; en.wikipedia gives no year at all; an earlier pass gave 1981, which is the year Erik af Klint died
stops.campa: Erik af Klint puts the collection into a foundation bearing his aunt's name, Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk: several thousand drawings and paintings together with the notebooks. The corpus survives because of it. A body of work no museum wanted now has a legal owner whose one purpose is to keep the paintings and the notebooks in one place. An earlier reading gave 1981 as the founding year; that is the year Erik af Klint died, not the year the foundation was made.
suggested_refs: Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk, the foundation holding the corpus and the notebooks

stops.name: Helsinki, Ake Fant reads the paper
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day of the Nordic conference not given in any source reached; pin at the city centre, venue unidentified
stops.campa: At a Nordic conference on art history in Helsinki the Swedish art historian Ake Fant shows af Klint's paintings to an international room for the first time. Forty years after her death and eighty-eight after the first automatic drawings, the work enters the discipline through a conference paper rather than through a gallery. The retrospectives and the rewritten first chapter of abstraction all date from this lecture hall. Fant follows the paper with a monograph, and neither text has been directly consulted here.
suggested_refs: Ake Fant's 1984 Nordic art-history conference paper on Hilma af Klint, Helsinki

stops.name: Los Angeles, The Spiritual in Art
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the November opening date is the exhibition's, not separately verified against an af Klint source
stops.campa: Her paintings hang at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art in The Spiritual in Art: Abstract Painting 1890-1985, the exhibition that put the occult back into the history of modernism and made Kandinsky, Mondrian, Malevich, and af Klint terms in one argument. It is her first major public exhibition context anywhere, forty-two years after her death and seventy-nine years after The Ten Largest were laid out on a studio floor in Stockholm. The wall label has to explain who she is, because no visitor arrives knowing.
suggested_refs: The Spiritual in Art: Abstract Painting 1890-1985, LACMA, 1986, and its catalogue

stops.name: Moderna Museet, Stockholm: A Pioneer of Abstraction
stops.date_confidence: attested as February to May 2013 at Moderna Museet, touring to Berlin, Malaga, Copenhagen, Oslo, and Tallinn through 2015; an earlier pass compressed the whole tour into 2013 and omitted the Stockholm launch
stops.campa: The museum that refused the gift in 1970 opens Hilma af Klint: A Pioneer of Abstraction, which runs from February to May and then travels to Berlin, Malaga, Copenhagen, Oslo, and Tallinn, continuing into 2015. Five years later the Foundation and the museum sign a long-term agreement establishing a permanent Hilma af Klint Room on Skeppsholmen. The refusal and the room are the same institution, forty-eight years apart, and nothing about the paintings changed in between.

stops.name: Venice, the Central Pavilion of the 55th Biennale
stops.date_confidence: year and pavilion attested; the June date is the Biennale's opening, day defaulted
stops.campa: Massimiliano Gioni puts af Klint in the Central Pavilion of the Giardini, at the entrance to Il Palazzo Enciclopedico, his Biennale built around outsider cosmologies and private systems of the world. She is placed there not as a footnote to Kandinsky but as one of the organising minds of the exhibition. In the same year the Stockholm retrospective is touring Europe, and the two together move her from rediscovery to canon. A hundred and seventeen years after the commission from Amaliel, the largest art exhibition in the world opens with her diagrams.

stops.campa: The Norwegian firm Snohetta presents plans for an exhibition building dedicated to af Klint at Jarna, south of Stockholm, in the country's anthroposophical heartland, with costs estimated at six to seven and a half million euros. Plans presented is all the record supports. No approving body is named in any source reached, and whether anything was ever built remains an open question. The original commission was for a temple, and no temple was built in her lifetime.

stops.date_confidence: attested as running 2018-2019; the October opening date is the museum's
stops.campa: Hilma af Klint: Paintings for the Future opens at the Solomon R. Guggenheim on Fifth Avenue, and Frank Lloyd Wright's spiral ramp turns out to be the room The Ten Largest were waiting for. Over six hundred thousand people come, the most-visited exhibition in the museum's sixty-year history. She had asked for a temple with an ascending spiral and had been given a rented studio on Hamngatan. The building arrives a hundred and twelve years after the commission.

stops.name: London, Tate Modern: Forms of Life
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the April opening date is the gallery's; an earlier pass described this as a solo af Klint exhibition, which it is not
stops.campa: Tate Modern hangs her with Piet Mondrian in Forms of Life, two painters who arrived at abstraction through theosophy and botany and who never met. It is not a solo retrospective, and the pairing is the point: af Klint is no longer being introduced but argued with, set against a canonical modernist as an equal term. Ninety-five years earlier she had shown these pictures in this city once, at a spiritualist conference, in a hall nobody has since been able to identify. Both London showings are on record; neither address is.
suggested_refs: Hilma af Klint & Piet Mondrian: Forms of Life, Tate Modern, London, 2023
